questions.q: What is the primary driver of tectonic plate movement?
questions.correct: Convection currents in the mantle
questions.why_correct: Heat from Earth's core creates circular loops of rising hot and sinking cool rock in the asthenosphere — these convection currents drag the plates along.
why_wrong: Earth's rotation is too slow and uniform to move individual tectonic plates.
The moon's gravity drives ocean tides, not tectonic plates — it is far too weak to move crustal rock.
While Earth has a magnetic field, it does not create forces strong enough to move tectonic plates.

questions.q: Why does magma rise from the mantle toward Earth's surface?
questions.correct: It is less dense than surrounding solid rock
incorrect: It is pushed upward by S-waves
It is pulled by Earth's magnetic field
It is heavier than the crust above it
questions.why_correct: Magma is less dense than the surrounding solid rock, so it rises buoyantly — the same reason a bubble rises through water.
why_wrong: S-waves are seismic waves from earthquakes — they do not push magma upward.
Earth's magnetic field originates in the outer core and does not attract or push magma.
Magma rises because it is lighter (less dense), not heavier, than the rock above it.

questions.q: Why does oceanic crust subduct beneath continental crust?
questions.correct: Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust
incorrect: Oceanic crust is thinner than continental crust
questions.why_correct: Oceanic basaltic crust is denser than continental granitic crust — at convergent boundaries the denser plate sinks beneath the lighter one.
why_wrong: While oceanic crust is often thinner, it is density — not thickness — that determines which plate subducts.
Plate speed varies and is not what determines subduction; density is the key factor.
Water content does not determine whether a plate subducts — density does.

questions.q: What feature forms at a divergent boundary on the ocean floor?
questions.correct: Mid-ocean ridge
questions.why_correct: At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart and magma rises to form new oceanic crust — building an underwater mountain range called a mid-ocean ridge.
why_wrong: Deep-sea trenches form at convergent (subduction) boundaries, not divergent ones.
Island arc volcanoes form when one oceanic plate subducts beneath another — a convergent process.
Mountain chains form when two continental plates collide — a convergent boundary feature.

questions.q: What features form at an oceanic-continental convergent boundary?
questions.correct: Deep-sea trench and volcanic mountains
incorrect: Island arc volcanoes and mid-ocean ridge
questions.why_correct: The dense oceanic plate sinks, forming a deep-sea trench. As it melts, magma rises through the overriding continental plate, creating volcanic mountains.
why_wrong: Mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys are features of divergent boundaries, where plates separate.
Island arc volcanoes form at oceanic-oceanic boundaries, not oceanic-continental ones.
Mountain chains form from continental-continental collisions; shield volcanoes form at hotspots.

questions.q: What forms when two continental plates collide?
questions.correct: Mountain chains
questions.why_correct: Neither plate subducts because both are too buoyant — the crust crumples and folds upward, building large mountain ranges like the Himalayas.
why_wrong: Deep-sea trenches require subduction of oceanic crust — continental plates are too buoyant to subduct.
Rift valleys form when a continental plate pulls apart at a divergent boundary, not when plates collide.
Island arc volcanoes form at oceanic-oceanic convergent boundaries, not continental collisions.

questions.q: What type of plate boundary has plates sliding horizontally past each other?
questions.correct: Transform boundary
questions.why_correct: At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other horizontally with no crust created or destroyed — the San Andreas Fault is a classic example.
why_wrong: Convergent boundaries involve plates moving toward and colliding with each other.
Divergent boundaries involve plates moving apart, not sliding past each other.
A subduction zone is a feature of convergent boundaries where one plate sinks beneath another.

questions.q: What type of volcano forms at a subduction zone?
questions.correct: Composite (explosive) volcano
questions.why_correct: At subduction zones, water from the descending plate lowers the melting point of mantle rock, producing silica-rich magma that erupts violently, building steep composite volcanoes.
why_wrong: Shield volcanoes form at hotspots and have calm, flowing lava eruptions — not associated with subduction.
Calderas result from magma chamber collapse and are not the primary type at subduction zones.
Cinder cone volcanoes are small and short-lived — not characteristic of subduction zones.

questions.q: What type of volcano forms at a hotspot?
questions.correct: Shield volcano
questions.why_correct: Hotspot magma is low in silica and flows easily, producing broad, flat shield volcanoes with calm lava flows — like those in Hawaii.
why_wrong: Composite volcanoes form at subduction zones where silica-rich magma causes explosive eruptions.
A stratovolcano is the same as a composite volcano and forms at subduction zones, not hotspots.
Cinder cone volcanoes are small and short-lived — shield volcanoes are the hotspot type.

questions.q: What is a hotspot?
questions.correct: A fixed magma pool beneath a plate, away from plate boundaries
incorrect: A magma chamber at a convergent boundary
A volcanic zone only at mid-ocean ridges
A transform fault with high volcanic activity
questions.why_correct: A hotspot is a stationary pool of magma in the mantle, fixed relative to the moving plate above it. As the plate moves, it creates a chain of progressively older volcanoes.
why_wrong: Hotspots are independent of plate boundaries — convergent boundaries have their own volcanic mechanisms.
Mid-ocean ridges form from divergent boundary activity, not hotspots.
Transform faults cause earthquake activity, not volcanic activity.

questions.q: What is sea-floor spreading?
questions.correct: New crust forming at mid-ocean ridges as plates pull apart
incorrect: Old crust recycled at deep-sea trenches
Sediment spreading across the ocean floor
Oceanic plates sliding past each other
questions.why_correct: At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart and magma rises to fill the gap, solidifying into new oceanic crust and widening the ocean basin over time.
why_wrong: Crust recycling at trenches is subduction — the opposite process from sea-floor spreading.
Sediment transport is a separate geological process unrelated to plate tectonics.
Plates sliding past each other describes transform boundaries, not sea-floor spreading.

questions.q: What forms when a continental plate pulls apart?
questions.correct: Rift valley
questions.why_correct: When tension pulls continental crust apart, the land between the faults drops to form a rift valley — which may eventually fill with water to become a new ocean.
why_wrong: Mountain chains form from compression when plates collide, not from tension pulling them apart.
Deep-sea trenches form at subduction zones, not at divergent continental boundaries.
Island arcs form when one oceanic plate subducts beneath another — a convergent process.

questions.q: What is the underground point where an earthquake originates?
questions.correct: The focus
questions.why_correct: The focus (also called the hypocenter) is the exact underground point where a fault slips and seismic energy is released.
why_wrong: The epicenter is on Earth's surface, directly above the focus — not underground.
The fault plane is the surface along which rocks slide, but the focus is the specific point of rupture.
Seismograph stations are surface instruments that detect earthquakes — not the origin point.

questions.q: What is the epicenter of an earthquake?
questions.correct: The point on the surface directly above the focus
incorrect: The underground origin point of the earthquake
The point where seismic damage is always worst
The center of the seismic shadow zone
questions.why_correct: The epicenter is always on Earth's surface, directly above the underground focus. It typically experiences the strongest shaking because it is closest to the energy source.
why_wrong: The underground origin point is the focus (hypocenter), not the epicenter.
While the epicenter often receives the strongest shaking, it is defined by its position above the focus.
The shadow zone is related to wave paths through Earth's core — not the epicenter.

questions.q: How many seismograph stations are needed to locate an epicenter?
questions.correct: Three
questions.why_correct: Each station produces a circle of possible locations. One circle gives many possibilities; two circles give two points; three circles narrow it to exactly one intersection point.
why_wrong: One station can only give a distance (a circle), not a direction — it cannot pinpoint the epicenter.
Two stations give two intersection points — you cannot determine which is correct without a third.
While more stations improve accuracy, three is the minimum needed to triangulate to a single point.

questions.q: Which seismic waves are fastest and arrive at a station first?
questions.correct: P-waves (primary waves)
questions.why_correct: P-waves are compressional waves that travel through both solids and liquids. They move fastest and always arrive at seismograph stations before S-waves.
why_wrong: S-waves are slower shear waves that follow P-waves — they always arrive second.
Surface waves travel along Earth's surface and are the slowest seismic waves, arriving last.
Love waves are a type of surface wave — they are slower than both P-waves and S-waves.

questions.q: Why can S-waves NOT travel through Earth's outer core?
questions.correct: The outer core is liquid, and S-waves only travel through solids
incorrect: The outer core is too hot for seismic waves
S-waves are absorbed by the inner core
The outer core is too dense for waves to pass through
questions.why_correct: S-waves are shear waves that require particles to move perpendicular to wave travel — only possible in solids. The liquid outer core cannot transmit this shear motion.
why_wrong: Temperature alone does not determine whether seismic waves can pass — the physical state (solid vs. liquid) is what matters.
S-waves stop at the outer core boundary; they are not absorbed by the inner core.
Density affects wave speed but does not stop waves — it is the liquid state, not density, that blocks S-waves.

questions.q: What does the seismic shadow zone tell us about Earth's interior?
questions.correct: Earth has a liquid outer core that blocks S-waves
incorrect: Earth has a solid inner core that absorbs all waves
The mantle is absent on the far side of Earth
S-waves are too weak to travel long distances
questions.why_correct: S-waves cannot travel through liquids. The shadow zone on the far side of Earth from an earthquake confirms that the outer core is liquid.
why_wrong: The inner core is solid — it actually transmits P-waves. The liquid outer core creates the shadow zone.
The mantle exists all the way around Earth — the shadow zone is caused by wave refraction and absorption in the core.
S-waves are not weak — they are stopped by the physical barrier of a liquid outer core, regardless of distance.

questions.q: What does a larger P-wave to S-wave time gap indicate?
questions.correct: The seismograph station is farther from the epicenter
incorrect: The station is in the shadow zone
questions.why_correct: P-waves are faster than S-waves and pull ahead over distance. A bigger time gap means more distance for P-waves to pull ahead, indicating a farther station.
why_wrong: Earthquake magnitude affects amplitude (wave height), not the relative timing between P and S waves.
The shadow zone is a region where S-waves don't arrive at all — not where there is just a gap.
P-waves always arrive first; S-waves are always second — the order never reverses.

questions.q: Which focus depth causes more severe surface damage for equal earthquake energy?
questions.correct: Shallow-focus earthquake
questions.why_correct: A shallow focus is close to the surface, so seismic energy reaches the ground before spreading and weakening. A deep-focus quake loses energy traveling through rock.
why_wrong: Deep-focus earthquakes release the same energy but farther from the surface, giving waves more distance to spread and weaken.
For equal energy, depth absolutely matters — a shallow earthquake delivers more energy to the surface.
While magnitude determines total energy released, depth determines how much energy reaches the surface — both factors matter.

questions.q: What stress causes a normal fault?
questions.correct: Tension (pulling apart)
questions.why_correct: Tension pulls the crust apart; the hanging wall drops down relative to the footwall as the rock on one side slips downward.
why_wrong: Compression causes reverse faults, where the hanging wall is pushed upward.
Shearing causes strike-slip faults, where rocks move past each other sideways.
Torsion is not one of the three primary fault-forming stresses in plate tectonics.

questions.q: In a normal fault, which direction does the hanging wall move?
questions.correct: Downward
incorrect: It does not move — only the footwall moves
questions.why_correct: In a normal fault, tension pulls the crust apart, and the hanging wall (the block above the fault plane) slides downward relative to the footwall below.
why_wrong: The hanging wall moving upward describes a reverse fault, caused by compression.
Horizontal movement describes a strike-slip fault — in normal faults, movement is vertical.
In a normal fault, the hanging wall definitely moves — it slides downward along the fault plane.

questions.q: What stress causes a reverse fault?
questions.correct: Compression (pushing together)
questions.why_correct: Compression squeezes the crust together, forcing the hanging wall to ride upward over the footwall — typical at convergent boundaries.
why_wrong: Tension causes normal faults, where the hanging wall drops down.
Shearing causes strike-slip faults, where rocks slide horizontally past each other.
Gravity drives mass movements like landslides, not the formation of reverse fault planes.

questions.q: The San Andreas Fault is an example of what?
questions.correct: A strike-slip fault at a transform boundary
incorrect: A reverse fault at a convergent boundary
A normal fault at a divergent boundary
A subduction zone at a convergent boundary
questions.why_correct: The San Andreas Fault is where the Pacific and North American plates slide horizontally past each other — a classic transform boundary with strike-slip motion.
why_wrong: A reverse fault involves vertical movement from compression — the San Andreas has horizontal, lateral motion.
Normal faults form where crust is pulled apart at divergent boundaries — the San Andreas involves lateral sliding.
The San Andreas Fault has no subduction — neither plate sinks beneath the other.

questions.q: What evidence supports the theory of continental drift?
questions.correct: Same fossils and rock types found on now-separated continents
incorrect: Different rock types on every continent
Ocean floor is the same age everywhere
All continents have the same climate today
questions.why_correct: Identical fossil species and matching rock formations on distant continents like Africa and South America indicate they were once joined and later drifted apart.
why_wrong: Different rock types on different continents would suggest they were always separate — identical rocks across oceans support drift.
The ocean floor is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and older toward trenches — it is not uniform age.
Different climates today are expected — it was tropical fossils in Antarctica and glacial marks in Africa that supported drift.

questions.q: Which of Earth's layers is thickest?
questions.correct: The mantle
questions.why_correct: The mantle extends from just below the crust to the outer core — roughly 2,900 km thick. It is the largest layer by volume.
why_wrong: The crust is the thinnest layer — only 5–70 km thick depending on whether it's oceanic or continental.
The outer core is thicker than the inner core but considerably thinner than the mantle.
The inner core is the deepest and smallest layer by volume.

questions.q: What two layers make up the lithosphere?
questions.correct: The crust and the rigid upper mantle
incorrect: The upper mantle and the outer core
The crust and the lower mantle
questions.why_correct: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell of Earth — it consists of the crust and the topmost rigid part of the mantle, forming the tectonic plates.
why_wrong: The asthenosphere is the plastic layer beneath the lithosphere, not part of it.
The outer core is deep within Earth and is liquid — it is not part of the lithosphere.
The lower mantle is below the asthenosphere — it is not part of the rigid lithosphere.

questions.q: How is the asthenosphere different from the lithosphere?
questions.correct: The asthenosphere is plastic and flows; the lithosphere is rigid
incorrect: The asthenosphere is solid; the lithosphere is liquid
The asthenosphere is in the crust; the lithosphere is in the core
They are the same layer with different names
questions.why_correct: The lithosphere (crust + rigid upper mantle) is brittle and breaks. The asthenosphere below it flows very slowly under pressure, allowing plates to move over it.
why_wrong: It is the opposite — the asthenosphere behaves plastically while the lithosphere is the rigid layer.
The asthenosphere is in the upper mantle, below the lithosphere — neither is in the core.
They are distinct layers with very different physical properties — rigid vs. plastic.

questions.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
questions.correct: The outer core
questions.why_correct: The outer core is composed of liquid iron and nickel. Its liquid state is confirmed by the seismic shadow zone — S-waves cannot pass through it.
why_wrong: The asthenosphere is plastic (semi-molten) and flows slowly, but it is technically solid under extreme pressure.
The inner core is solid iron — held solid by immense pressure despite being hotter than the outer core.
The lower mantle is solid rock under extreme pressure — it does not flow as a liquid.

questions.q: Why do the Hawaiian Islands get progressively older farther from the Big Island?
questions.correct: The Pacific plate moved over a fixed hotspot, leaving older islands behind
incorrect: The Big Island formed first and the plate built outward from it
Erosion makes distant islands appear older
The hotspot drifts southeastward over time
questions.why_correct: The hotspot is stationary. As the Pacific plate moves northwestward over it, new volcanoes form above the hotspot; older islands are carried away and are progressively older.
why_wrong: The Big Island is the youngest island, formed most recently as the plate moved over the hotspot.
Erosion affects island size and shape but does not change the actual age of volcanic rock.
Hotspots are fixed in the mantle — it is the plate that moves, not the hotspot.

questions.q: What seismogram features indicate a station is closest to the epicenter?
questions.correct: Small P-to-S wave gap and large wave amplitude
incorrect: Large P-to-S wave gap and small amplitude
questions.why_correct: A close station receives waves that have traveled less distance — P and S waves are still close together in time, and more energy arrives before it spreads out.
why_wrong: A large P-to-S gap and small amplitude indicates a distant station, not a close one.
Only P-waves with no S-waves is the signature of a shadow zone station far on the opposite side of Earth.
All stations within range record waves — stations in the shadow zone record only P-waves.

questions.q: At what type of boundary does sea-floor spreading occur?
questions.correct: Divergent boundary (oceanic plates pulling apart)
questions.why_correct: Sea-floor spreading requires plates to move apart, allowing magma to rise and create new crust — this happens at divergent boundaries at mid-ocean ridges.
why_wrong: At convergent boundaries, crust is destroyed through subduction — the opposite of spreading.
Transform boundaries involve sideways sliding — no crust is created or destroyed.
At oceanic-continental convergent boundaries, oceanic crust subducts — it is destroyed, not created.

questions.q: What mountain range formed from the Indian and Eurasian plate collision?
questions.correct: The Himalayas
questions.why_correct: When India collided with Eurasia about 50 million years ago, neither plate subducted — the crust crumpled upward into the Himalayas, Earth's highest mountain range.
why_wrong: The Andes formed from the subduction of the Nazca oceanic plate beneath South America — a different process.
The Rocky Mountains formed from oceanic plate subduction beneath North America — not a continental collision.
The Alps formed from the collision of the African and Eurasian plates — not the Indian-Eurasian collision.

questions.q: What information does a seismograph use to calculate its circle's radius for triangulation?
questions.correct: Time difference between P-wave and S-wave arrivals
questions.why_correct: P-waves are faster and arrive before S-waves. The time gap between them corresponds to the distance to the epicenter — a bigger gap means a farther station and larger circle radius.
why_wrong: A seismograph records wave arrivals but cannot determine direction — that's why multiple stations are needed.
S-wave amplitude indicates earthquake magnitude, not distance from the epicenter.
Temperature is irrelevant to seismic wave travel time calculations.

questions.q: Why do most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries?
questions.correct: Plate boundaries are where friction, stress, and sudden rock slipping occur
incorrect: Plate boundaries have thinner crust that breaks more easily
Seismographs are only located near plate boundaries
All earthquakes occur at convergent boundaries only
questions.why_correct: Where plates grind past, collide, or pull apart, stress builds in the rocks. When it exceeds the rock's strength, it releases suddenly as seismic energy.
why_wrong: While oceanic crust is thinner, all crust types experience earthquakes at boundaries — thickness alone is not the cause.
Seismographs are located worldwide — earthquake detection is not limited to plate boundaries.
Earthquakes occur at all three boundary types — convergent, divergent, and transform.

questions.q: What forms when two oceanic plates collide?
questions.correct: Deep-sea trench and island arc volcanoes
questions.why_correct: When two oceanic plates converge, the denser one subducts — creating a deep-sea trench where it sinks and a curved chain of volcanic islands above the subduction zone.
why_wrong: Mountain chains form from continental-continental collision; rift valleys form at divergent boundaries.
Shield volcanoes form at hotspots; mid-ocean ridges form at divergent boundaries.
Normal faults and rift valleys form at divergent boundaries where crust is being stretched.

questions.q: At a divergent continental boundary, what eventually forms if spreading continues?
questions.correct: A new ocean (begins as a rift valley)
questions.why_correct: Continental rifting first creates a rift valley; as spreading continues, the valley sinks below sea level, fills with water, and becomes a new ocean — like the early Atlantic.
why_wrong: Mountain ranges require compression — plate collision. Rifting is the opposite process: extension.
Island arcs require subduction of oceanic plates — they do not result from continental divergence.
Subduction zones require a dense oceanic plate to sink — they do not form at divergent boundaries.

questions.q: What is the difference between the hanging wall and footwall of a fault?
questions.correct: The hanging wall is above the fault plane; the footwall is below
incorrect: The footwall is above the fault plane; the hanging wall is below
They are the same — just different names for each side
The hanging wall only exists in reverse faults
questions.why_correct: The fault plane is a diagonal crack. The hanging wall is the block that 'hangs' above the plane; the footwall is the block you could stand on below the plane.
why_wrong: It is the reverse — the hanging wall is always above the fault plane, the footwall below.
They are distinct — both exist in all inclined fault types (normal, reverse, and thrust faults).
Both hanging wall and footwall are present in all inclined fault types, not just reverse faults.

questions.q: Why is the asthenosphere important for plate tectonics?
questions.correct: Its plastic flow allows tectonic plates to move over it
incorrect: It generates heat that melts the core
questions.why_correct: The asthenosphere is partially molten and flows very slowly. The rigid lithospheric plates ride on top and are dragged by convection currents within it.
why_wrong: The asthenosphere does not generate the heat driving tectonics — that comes from the core and radioactive decay.
Most earthquakes originate in the lithosphere (crust and rigid upper mantle), not the asthenosphere.
Earth's magnetic field is generated by liquid iron movement in the outer core, not the asthenosphere.

questions.q: Which type of plate boundary does NOT create or destroy crust?
questions.correct: Transform boundary
questions.why_correct: At transform boundaries, plates simply slide past each other horizontally — no new crust forms and no crust is subducted or destroyed.
why_wrong: Divergent boundaries create new crust as magma fills the gap between separating plates.
Convergent boundaries destroy crust through subduction — the denser plate melts in the mantle.
A subduction zone is a type of convergent boundary — oceanic crust is destroyed as it sinks.

questions.q: A seismogram shows only a P-wave with no S-wave. What does this indicate?
questions.correct: The station is in the seismic shadow zone
incorrect: The station is closest to the epicenter
S-waves were absorbed by the crust
questions.why_correct: The shadow zone is a region where S-waves are blocked by the liquid outer core. Only P-waves — which can travel through liquids — arrive in this zone.
why_wrong: All significant earthquakes produce both P-waves and S-waves — they cannot produce only one type.
The closest station would receive both P and S waves with a small time gap — not just P-waves.
S-waves travel through the crust and mantle fine — they are blocked by the liquid outer core, not the crust.

questions.q: What is the ultimate energy source driving plate tectonics?
questions.correct: Heat from Earth's core and radioactive decay in the mantle
questions.why_correct: Heat from Earth's formation and ongoing radioactive decay in the mantle powers convection currents — the mechanism that moves tectonic plates.
why_wrong: Solar radiation heats only the very surface and atmosphere — it does not penetrate deep enough to drive mantle convection.
The moon's gravity drives tidal forces in the ocean — not the mantle convection that moves plates.
Chemical reactions in the crust are too shallow and weak to power the large-scale convection driving tectonics.

questions.q: At which boundary type is the youngest ocean floor rock found?
questions.correct: Divergent boundary (mid-ocean ridge)
questions.why_correct: New oceanic crust is constantly being created at mid-ocean ridges. Rock right at the ridge is the youngest — age increases as you move away in both directions.
why_wrong: At convergent (subduction) zones, the oldest oceanic crust is being destroyed — not where young rock is found.
Transform boundaries neither create nor destroy crust — no new rock forms there.
Continental-continental boundaries form mountain ranges — no oceanic crust is created there.

questions.q: All of the following are features of convergent boundaries EXCEPT:
questions.correct: Mid-ocean ridge
questions.why_correct: Mid-ocean ridges form at divergent boundaries, where plates pull apart and magma rises. They are not a feature of convergent boundaries.
why_wrong: Deep-sea trenches form at convergent boundaries — where the denser plate subducts.
Volcanic mountains form at oceanic-continental convergent boundaries as subducted rock melts.
Island arc volcanoes form at oceanic-oceanic convergent boundaries.

questions.q: All of the following are true about P-waves EXCEPT:
questions.correct: They cannot travel through Earth's liquid outer core
incorrect: They travel through both solids and liquids
questions.why_correct: P-waves CAN travel through the liquid outer core — that's why they appear on the far side of Earth. It is S-waves that are blocked by the liquid outer core.
why_wrong: P-waves do arrive first — they are the fastest seismic waves.
P-waves do travel through both solids and liquids — that is one of their defining characteristics.
P-waves are faster than S-waves — that is why they are called 'primary' waves.

questions.q: What happens to oceanic crust at a mid-ocean ridge?
questions.correct: New oceanic crust is created as magma rises and solidifies
incorrect: Old oceanic crust sinks into the mantle
Two plates slide past each other
Continental crust converts to oceanic crust
questions.why_correct: At mid-ocean ridges, diverging plates create a gap that fills with rising magma. The magma cools and hardens into new basaltic oceanic crust.
why_wrong: Crust sinking into the mantle describes subduction at trenches — the opposite end of the plate cycle.
Plates sliding past each other describes transform boundaries, not mid-ocean ridges.
Oceanic and continental crust have different compositions — one does not convert into the other.

questions.q: Which layer of Earth generates its magnetic field?
questions.correct: The liquid outer core
questions.why_correct: The movement of liquid iron in the outer core generates electric currents that produce Earth's magnetic field — acting like a dynamo.
why_wrong: The inner core is solid iron — solid material cannot flow in the way needed to generate a magnetic field.
The asthenosphere is partly molten rock (silicate minerals), not iron — it does not generate a significant magnetic field.
The crust is too thin and contains too little iron to generate Earth's global magnetic field.

questions.q: What information does each station use to calculate the size of its triangulation circle?
questions.correct: The P-wave to S-wave arrival time difference
incorrect: The direction the waves came from
questions.why_correct: The time gap between the faster P-wave and slower S-wave tells each station how far away it is from the epicenter — a larger gap means a larger circle.
why_wrong: Seismographs record wave arrival times, not direction — that's why three stations are needed.
Wave amplitude tells you how much energy arrived, not how far away the source was.
The number of waves indicates ongoing seismic activity, not the distance to the epicenter.

questions.q: What occurs at a subduction zone where the descending plate melts?
questions.correct: Magma forms and rises to create volcanoes on the overriding plate
incorrect: The plates bounce back and form mountains without volcanoes
The melted rock forms a new ocean ridge
The melt stays in the mantle and never surfaces
questions.why_correct: As the subducting plate descends and melts, water lowers the melting point of surrounding mantle rock. Less-dense magma forms and rises through the overriding plate as volcanoes.
why_wrong: Plates at subduction zones do not 'bounce back' — one continuously sinks into the mantle.
Ocean ridges form at divergent boundaries where plates pull apart — not at subduction zones.
At subduction zones, magma routinely rises to the surface, creating volcanic arcs or mountain ranges.

questions.q: What happens when two oceanic plates collide and one subducts?
questions.correct: A deep-sea trench and island arc form above the subduction zone
incorrect: Both plates fold upward into a mountain range
The plates begin sliding past each other
New oceanic crust forms between them
questions.why_correct: When two oceanic plates converge, the denser plate subducts into the mantle — forming a deep-sea trench where it sinks and a curved volcanic island arc above it.
why_wrong: Mountain ranges form from continental-continental collisions — oceanic plates are too dense to fold upward like that.
Sliding past each other describes transform boundaries — not what happens when plates converge and collide.
New crust forms at divergent boundaries — at convergent boundaries, crust is being destroyed.

terms.definition: Drives convection currents in the mantle, which move tectonic plates.
Circular loops of hot rising and cool sinking rock in the asthenosphere; the force that moves tectonic plates.
At subduction zones, descending plates melt from extreme heat and pressure, forming magma.

terms.term: less dense magma rises through the mantle
terms.definition: Magma is less dense than solid rock, so it rises buoyantly toward the surface.
Oceanic (basaltic) crust is denser than continental crust, causing it to subduct at convergent boundaries.
Curved chain of volcanic islands formed when one oceanic plate subducts beneath another.
Mountains formed by magma rising through the crust at convergent boundaries.
Formed when two continental plates collide and compress, forcing rock upward (e.g., the Himalayas).
Underwater mountain range at a divergent boundary where magma rises and forms new oceanic crust.
Long, narrow ocean-floor depression where one plate subducts beneath another at a convergent boundary.
Where a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate into the mantle.
New oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges as plates separate and magma fills the gap.
A valley formed when a continental plate pulls apart; may eventually become a new ocean.
Tectonic plates are constantly in motion due to convection currents in the mantle.
A fixed pool of magma beneath a plate that creates volcanoes at the surface, independent of plate boundaries (e.g., Hawaii).
Where two oceanic plates meet; forms trenches, island arc volcanoes (convergent) or mid-ocean ridges (divergent).
Where oceanic plate subducts beneath continental plate; forms deep-sea trenches and volcanic mountains.
Where two continental plates collide; forms large mountain ranges.
Two plates move toward each other and collide.
Two plates move apart; magma rises to form new crust.
Two plates slide horizontally past each other; no crust created or destroyed.
Continental plate pulls apart, forming a rift valley that may fill with water to become a new sea.
Steep, layered volcano at subduction zones; violent explosive eruptions.

terms.term: What evidence supports the theory of continental drift?
terms.definition: Same rocks and fossils found on different continents; continents fit together like puzzle pieces; glaciers in now-tropical areas (evidence of past tropical climates near the poles).

terms.term: List the layers of Earth in order from the surface, including minor layers.
terms.definition: Crust → lithosphere (crust + upper mantle) → asthenosphere (upper mantle) → lower mantle → outer core → inner core.

terms.term: What two layers make up the lithosphere?
terms.definition: The crust and the very top layer of the mantle.

terms.term: How is the asthenosphere different from the lithosphere?
terms.definition: The asthenosphere is plastic — it flows very slowly like a solid under extreme pressure. The lithosphere above it is rigid and brittle.

terms.term: List Earth's layers in order from thinnest to thickest.
terms.definition: Crust (thinnest) → inner core → outer core → mantle (thickest).

terms.term: What force causes tectonic plates to move?
terms.definition: Convection currents in the asthenosphere — hot rock rises, cools, sinks, and cycles in loops that drag the plates along.

terms.term: What happens at an oceanic-oceanic convergent boundary, and what features form?
terms.definition: The plates collide; the denser plate subducts. This forms deep-sea trenches and island arc volcanoes.

terms.term: What forms when two continental plates collide?
terms.definition: Mountain chains — neither plate subducts, so the crust crumples and folds upward (e.g., the Himalayas).

terms.term: What happens at a divergent boundary, and what features form?
terms.definition: Plates move apart; magma rises to fill the gap, forming new crust. This creates mid-ocean ridges (underwater) or rift valleys (on land).

terms.term: The San Andreas Fault is an example of what type of plate boundary?
terms.definition: Transform — the two plates slide horizontally past each other. No crust is created or destroyed.

terms.term: Why do oceanic plates subduct beneath continental plates?
terms.definition: Oceanic (basaltic) crust is denser than continental crust, so it sinks beneath the lighter continental plate at convergent boundaries.

terms.term: At what type of plate boundary is the youngest ocean floor rock found, and why?
terms.definition: Divergent boundaries — new oceanic crust is constantly being created as magma rises and solidifies at mid-ocean ridges.

terms.term: What mountain range was formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates?
terms.definition: The Himalayas — two continental plates collided, and neither subducted, forcing the crust upward into the highest mountain range on Earth.
At mid-ocean ridges, plates move apart and magma rises to form new oceanic crust, pushing the existing ocean floor outward and making the ocean wider over time.

terms.term: At what type of boundary does sea-floor spreading occur?
terms.definition: Oceanic-oceanic divergent boundary — two oceanic plates pull apart and new crust forms at the ridge between them.

terms.term: What is the difference between the epicenter and the focus of an earthquake?
terms.definition: The focus is the underground point where the fault actually slips and energy is released. The epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus.

terms.term: Which seismic waves are fastest and arrive at a seismograph station first?
terms.definition: P-waves (primary waves) — they travel through both solids and liquids and are the fastest seismic waves.

terms.term: Why do most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries?
terms.definition: Plate boundaries are where plates grind past, collide, or pull apart. The friction and stress build up and are suddenly released as seismic energy.

terms.term: Why are earthquakes felt more strongly at the epicenter than farther away?
terms.definition: The epicenter is directly above the focus where energy is released. Closer locations receive more energy before it spreads out and weakens over distance.

terms.term: Which causes more severe surface damage: a shallow-focus or deep-focus earthquake of equal energy? Why?
terms.definition: Shallow-focus — the focus is close to the surface, so less energy is lost before the waves reach the ground. Deep-focus quakes lose more energy traveling through rock.

terms.term: Normal fault: stress type and wall movement.
terms.definition: Caused by tension (pulling apart). The hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall.

terms.term: Reverse fault: stress type and wall movement.
terms.definition: Caused by compression (pushing together). The hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall.

terms.term: Strike-slip fault: stress type and rock movement.
terms.definition: Caused by shearing (sideways). Rocks slide horizontally past each other with no up or down movement (e.g., San Andreas Fault).

terms.term: Why does magma from Earth's interior rise toward the surface?
terms.definition: Magma is less dense than the surrounding solid rock, so it rises buoyantly — the same reason a bubble rises through water.

terms.term: What is a hot spot, and where is it located relative to plate boundaries?
terms.definition: A hot spot is a fixed pool of magma beneath a plate that creates volcanoes at the surface. It is independent of plate boundaries — randomly located away from the edges (e.g., Hawaii).

terms.term: What type of volcano forms at a hot spot?
terms.definition: Shield volcanoes — broad and flat with calm, flowing lava eruptions (e.g., the Hawaiian volcanoes).

terms.term: How does the age of the Hawaiian Islands relate to their distance from the active hot spot?
terms.definition: The Big Island (Hawaii) is youngest and directly over the hot spot. Islands get progressively older as you move away — the plate moved over the fixed hot spot, creating a chain.
